n: Woe to Nineveh, the city of bloodshed, full of lies and plunder, never letting go of its victims. Assyria was infamous for brutality against conquered peoples.
Nahum paints a battle scene with sounds: cracking whips, rumbling wheels, galloping horses, bouncing chariots.
Flashing swords and glittering spears; bodies pile up so high that soldiers stumble over them. Assyria’s own violence returns on it.
Nineveh is pictured as a seductive prostitute and sorceress who lured and enslaved nations by charm, trade, and deception.

f.g: An attractive prostitute — a symbol of seductive power and trade.

n: “I am against you,” says the Lord. He will expose Nineveh’s shame before all nations, as a disgraced woman was publicly exposed.

f.g: Lift up your skirts — expose you.

f.w: I will shew the nations thy nakedness

n: God will throw filth on her and make her a public spectacle.

f.g: An object to be stared at in contempt.

n: Everyone who sees Nineveh will run away, saying, “It’s ruined! Who will mourn for her?” No one will comfort her.
Are you better than Thebes? That great Egyptian city on the Nile, protected by water, fell to Assyria itself in 663 BC.

f.g: No-Amon, Thebes in Upper Egypt (near modern Luxor).
The Nile, wide like a sea.

n: Thebes had powerful allies — Ethiopia, Egypt, Put, and Libya — and seemingly limitless strength.

f.g: Cush, the kingdom south of Egypt, which ruled Egypt at that time.
Peoples of North Africa; Lubim are Libyans.

n: Yet Thebes was captured: children killed, nobles divided by lottery, leaders put in chains. What Assyria did to others will be done to Assyria.

f.w: they cast lots for her honourable men

n: Nineveh too will stagger as if drunk, hide, and search for refuge from the enemy.
Its fortresses will fall as easily as ripe figs drop into a mouth when the tree is shaken.

f.g: Early figs, which fall at the slightest shake.

n: Nineveh’s soldiers will be weak and helpless, its gates wide open, its bars burned.

f.w: thy people in the midst of thee are women
f.g: An ancient insult meaning the troops will be powerless.

n: Ironic advice: stock up water for the siege, strengthen your forts, make more bricks! None of it will matter.

f.g: Mix mud and straw with the feet to make bricks.

n: Fire and sword will consume Nineveh like locusts devour a field. Even if Nineveh multiplies like locusts, it will not survive.

f.g: A kind of locust in its young stage.

n: Nineveh’s merchants were as countless as stars, but like locusts they strip the land and fly away.

f.g: Sheds its skin and flies off.

n: Assyria’s officials are like locusts huddled in a hedge on a cold day; when the sun comes out they vanish without a trace.
Speaking directly to Assyria’s king: your shepherds (leaders) sleep in death, your nobles lie in the dust, and your people are scattered with no one to gather them.
Your wound is fatal. Everyone who hears of your fall will clap with joy — for who has not suffered from your endless cruelty? Assyria never recovered after 612 BC.
